title: Dressing the Man
creator: Alan Flusser
note: The foundation: the rules and proportions of classic menswear. The creator calls it his starting point.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
chapters: Accessories: the major importance of minor things
contents.coverage: Adapting classic clothing to individual physique and complexion; coordinating patterns, choosing silhouettes and collars, and dressing for business casual and formal occasions.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Practical notes across 12 headings; formalwear thin. Core ideas corroborated by established reviews, finer rules mostly from reader notes.
knowledge.limits: No full chapters read. F3 is a secondary reader-note source, not a publisher excerpt. Its measurements and rules are reported advice, not independently authenticated text or universal fitting laws.

sections.summary: Start with the wearer, not seasonal fashion. The stable relationships of face, neck, shoulders, torso and legs are a better foundation than designer novelty. Interwar examples teach principles rather than require historical imitation. GQ notes that the book does not fully address modern casual lifestyles.

Keep attention on the face. F3 describes relating clothing contrast to actual hair/skin contrast and repeating natural pigments near the face. Strong contrast can support a high-contrast face but overwhelm a muted one. Assess the individual, not an ethnic category. Reviews corroborate complexion as a central concern, not every precise color prescription.

GQ quotes the relation between broader shoulders and fuller lapels. Collar-to-face, shoulders-to-head and jacket-to-leg relationships must be judged together. F3 says narrow shoulders exaggerate head size and broad shoulders diminish it. Cover the seat without needlessly shortening the apparent leg. There is no single fashionable jacket length appropriate to everyone.

F3 reports strongly different scales for two similar patterns; compatible scale for unlike patterns; and avoiding two tiny busy designs. With three similar patterns, graduate size from the shirt outward. With two similar and one unlike, separate the similar scales and relate the odd design to the prominent one. The aim is a readable whole, not showing how many patterns you can combine.

F1 reports 0.5-0.75 inch of shirt collar above the jacket collar. F3 says trouser volume should continue the jacket silhouette: fuller jackets with fuller trousers, closer jackets with slimmer legs. It favors trousers at the waist, charcoal as a versatile first business suit and navy as flattering. These are classic business priorities, not every wardrobe's needs.

Darker trousers can dress up a sport jacket. Color can unify separates: keep two of three pieces in the same family and relate the shirt through tone or contrast. A waistcoat adds gravity to single-breasted tailoring. This is an incomplete secondary account, not the full chapter.

Choose collar shape for the face. F3 describes spread points as a counterweight to a long narrow face, collar size relative to head size and collar height relative to neck length. Allow room to sit and raise arms without gaping or untucking. Cuffs should stay at the wrist, not slide over the hand. Smooth cloth and firmer collars read dressier; choose a blue that supports rather than overwhelms the face.

Tie width relates to lapels. F3 places the knot within the collar opening and the tip near the belt's upper edge. F1 specifically records the advised dimple. F3 limits bow width to the face/collar scale. Balance matters more than buying the fashionable width or largest knot.

Relate socks to trousers rather than make sock and shoe into an isolated block. Another option repeats a color or pattern from near the face. Finer hosiery suits more formal clothes; bulkier textures support heavier socks. The notes' restriction on black socks is a traditional preference, not a universal current rule.

F1 confirms smart shoes with tailored trousers. F3 describes a cap-toe Oxford for smart town wear, a blucher as less dressy and brown suede across seasons. Shape, formality, condition and relation to the trouser matter. Unsupported spending or leather-age claims are not adopted.

sections.section: Accessories: the major importance of minor things
sections.summary: Echo rather than exactly match a tie with the square. A lustrous tie can benefit from matte linen/cotton; a square can pick up a shirt or jacket color. Keep the effect unstudied. Belt color follows shoes and then the outfit, with a simple buckle. Details support the whole rather than pull attention away from the face.

The review confirms distinctions between dinner-jacket and full-dress details. Reliable actual chapter rules were not recovered. Rules from another book or a generic black-tie guide are not substituted and labeled Flusser.

A shared color family holds unmatched separates together; a patterned shirt can repeat a jacket/trouser color. F4 questions the longevity of a near-monochrome polo-and-corduroy example. The 2002 chapter's coordination logic travels better than every outfit or workplace assumption.

title: True Style
creator: G. Bruce Boyer
note: Commentary on wardrobe pieces, their history and how to wear them. The creator returns to Boyer’s ideas often.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
contents.coverage: Alphabetically arranged essays on wardrobe pieces, traditions, fabrics, patterns, colors and how to use them, combining history with practical style advice.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Substantive or historical notes on 24 of 26 essays, with uneven depth. Boots and dressing gowns unverified; shorts and craftsmanship remain thin.
knowledge.limits: Established reviews corroborate the core philosophy; much chapter detail relies on two openly posted reader-note sources, not an official complete preview. Care advice remains subject to garment labels and professional judgment.

sections.summary: The name comes from the Ascot race meeting and its pinned silk neck scarf. B4 presents soft silk/light cashmere at an open collar as an alternative to a bare neck. This establishes a tradition and option, not the entire essay.
No reliable substantive account of this essay was recovered.
Boyer prefers a self-tied rather than pre-tied bow. Its irregular natural shape belongs to wearing it, rather than requiring factory-perfect symmetry.

Clothes communicate membership and context. Aim to let others judge your work instead of your outfit. Simplicity and comfort matter; head-to-toe designer outfits and conspicuous matching can erase individuality. B3's country-jacket/jeans and Barbour/suit examples illustrate mixing genres, not what every office permits.

Quality may cost more initially but last longer. The essay's craft discussion includes Thomas Girtin's Makers of Distinction and Richard Sennett's The Craftsman as reading. No full construction checklist was recovered.
The essay moves from workwear to youth rebellion, including Brando in The Wild One. Clothing carries a social language beyond its material. No complete fit/wash advice recovered.
No reliable substantive account of this essay was recovered.

Accumulated, lived-in clothes and patina suggest continuity rather than a freshly purchased coordinated costume. Sturdy country fabrics and pieces of different ages can look at ease together. The point is an unforced whole, not mandatory shabbiness.

Matching coat/trousers, uncuffed hems and an outside stripe related to lapel facings make a coherent tuxedo. The silk bow relates to those facings. Plain dark hosiery and simple black footwear keep focus on the wearer. The notes list calf/patent Oxfords and formal slippers as options; this is not the complete essay.

Frames should fit within the face width, sit below eyebrows and above cheeks, and stay securely on the bridge. They support the intended impression without becoming the main subject. Optical fit and prescription requirements still need an optician.

Know scent type and strength; use a restrained amount in business and lighter scents in heat. Test on skin and wait before judging. Avoid sun, unsealed storage and extreme temperatures. Aim for a clean presence rather than a scent cloud.
Facial hair is personal choice within professional context, not a blanket requirement to shave. Relate beard/moustache volume to face size so it does not become a detached dominating feature.

Lighter construction can retain shape. The account connects Armani's reduced padding with comfort and describes the lighter Neapolitan approach. It distinguishes more sober northern business dress from playful combinations. National generalizations do not prescribe every person's style.

Oxford button-down, khakis, Shetland sweater and loafers form an adaptable core. Tweed/navy blazer, flannel suits and seasonal suits increase formality. Edge stitching is one jacket marker. The lesson is a compatible vocabulary, not an obligatory shopping list.

Rotate and air clothes; brush tailored cloth, fold knitwear, use proper hangers and shoe trees. Avoid needless dry cleaning/pressing; use cautious heat and a protective cloth if the garment permits. Sleeve/trouser adjustments are unlike rebuilding shoulders/collar/chest: buy near a good base fit. Follow the actual care label before applying any technique.

Personality and deliberate choice matter more than rigid correctness. Clothes complement you; quality matters; refusing a distracting purchase is part of style. Avoid displaying money, accessories or rule memorization.

Prevent one garment dominating. Vary scales so pieces remain legible. Subtle pattern against pattern can integrate an outfit better than isolating one loud design against stark solids. Judge the whole, not a pattern count.
Restrained silk gives business dress a small accent; white linen/cotton is a simple formal option. Tie and square echo rather than exactly match. A related color is more relaxed than a matching set.

B1 reports smaller collars for smaller men and higher collars for longer necks. B4 relates knot size to tie space, collar stiffness to formality and sleeves so about half an inch of cuff shows. Treat collar/tie/square as one chest composition; exact matching can look labored.

Boyer objects to sockless business suits with dress shoes. B4 describes footwear as either continuing the leg line or deliberately breaking it, with darker shoes coherent against trousers and brown offering tonal variety. This is not a ban on all sockless casual wear.
The essay connects shorts to military/sporting dress. Its actual length, styling and occasion advice was not recovered.

Conceal effort, rather than be ignorant or careless. A little rumple or unforced genre mixing can look more convincing than flawless coordination. Do not mechanically add a contrived mistake; ease comes from understanding what you wear.

A commissioned waistcoat adds variations, pockets and temperature flexibility. Peak lapels are the traditional double-breasted choice. The notes establish selected ideas and historical development, not a complete fit/fabric manual.

Linen, breathable wool and deliberately rumpled seersucker have different useful behaviors. Choose for climate and cloth performance rather than demand permanent sharp pressing. The essay treats wrinkles as compatible with summer ease.
A turtleneck with a suit is permitted as deliberate nonchalance in a suitable setting. Its bohemian associations are discussed. It does not replace required formal attire at every occasion.

Bonded rubber/cotton, tightly woven treated gabardine and waxed cotton are distinct traditions. Waxed cloth requires renewed wax. Heritage and material history do not establish a modern technical waterproof rating.

title: Modern Black Tie: A Guide
creator: Mickael Korausch
note: An actionable guide to evening wear and building a traditional or alternative black-tie kit, rather than a history-only read.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
contents.status: Publisher-confirmed structure; exact chapter names not verified
contents.coverage: Ten chapters, a black-tie brand directory and a Stephen Fry foreword. Covers classic and contemporary evening wear, outfit/accessory examples across levels of formality, and the future of the dress code.
contents.caveat: The official preview page was found, but its contents pages were not readable in this check. Do not treat this coverage summary as a complete table of contents.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Detailed practical topic notes from official companion guides. Direct book evidence limited to its philosophy and ten-chapter structure.
knowledge.limits: Exact chapter titles and mapping remain unverified. M2/M3 are author-site companion articles, not proven book excerpts. Their color recommendations and shawl-lapel history conflict. Product description says 300+ pages, another article 400+; no edition claim made.

sections.summary: Black tie evolves. The book respects traditional tenets while emphasizing the effort made for special occasions. It presents different formality levels and alternatives. This is not permission to ignore an invitation's actual expectations.

Single-breasted one-button peak/shawl and double-breasted alternatives are presented. Silk lapel facings and jetted pockets distinguish eveningwear from business suits. M3 rejects notch lapels as a house preference. M2 calls no vents traditional but permits other vents, and relates broader lapels to double-breasted balance.

Satin is smooth and reflective; grosgrain ribbed and more matte. M2 relates finer ribs to curved shawls and stronger ribs to peaks; self-facings suit velvet/less overtly formal jackets. M3 discusses barathea and wool-mohair. Its body praises midnight blue but FAQ favors black. That conflict is not turned into a single rule.

Higher rise and enough leg volume support a clean vertical line. Classic trousers match jacket cloth with silk outside-seam trim and uncuffed hem. M3 excludes belts, favors braces and recommends waistcoat or cummerbund, not both. Its blanket waist-covering statement does not explain double-breasted exceptions; these are not inferred as book content.

Marcella/piqué fronts provide formal texture with studs; pleated fronts add texture with studs or suitable buttons; covered plackets offer quiet minimalism. The aim is differentiation from a daily business shirt. Full collar/cuff advice not recovered.

A self-tied silk bow relates to lapel facing; a simple white square and socks covering skin when seated complete the outfit. M2 favors coherent studs/cufflinks over competing details. Its shirt-studs subsection is visibly incomplete, so not summarized.

Tartan with velvet, checks with off-white jackets and velvet-on-velvet are presented as alternatives. White trousers are called summer-only and nontraditional. Smoking/velvet jackets suit some less strict events. Distinguish experimentation from the classic uniform and follow the invitation.

Ready-to-wear fixes standard proportions; made-to-measure adjusts an existing pattern; bespoke creates an individual pattern through fittings. The site's preference for its own made-to-measure service is commercial, not an objective universal ranking. Ask what can actually be changed.

The Beaux on the Row: Men Who Led Fashion

Savile Row in Hollywood: Aristocrats of the Silver Screen

contents.coverage: Chronological tailoring history through customers, monarchy, military, film and revival; 26 master-tailor profiles plus reference sections on suit anatomy and making.
contents.caveat: The publisher describes eight chronological themes, while the bookseller list has six numbered sections plus references. The library catalog gives only a partial list. Preserve this source mismatch rather than inventing two missing chapters.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Concrete historical/craft ideas from publisher and two established reviews, but limited chapter depth.
knowledge.limits: This is primarily social/house history. Permanent Style warns it is not a current tailor-selection guide. Existing contents mismatch remains. Historical house/service details are not current availability.

sections.summary: Early bespoke drew from the restrained English country gentleman's wardrobe. The publisher follows aristocratic to military patronage. This explains the prestige of sobriety and individual fit; complete monarch-specific chapter detail was not recovered.

House histories emerge through customers, including film clients of Anderson & Sheppard and naval associations at Gieves & Hawkes. Cut/reputation and social context are connected. That does not prove one house cut suits everyone or describe current service. Full detail of these chapters remains unavailable.

Hawkes introduced immediate wear in 1929; its off-the-peg sales surpassed bespoke by 1948. The review names Richard Anderson, Ozwald Boateng and Richard James as a new establishment, and Edward Sexton, Spencer Hart and Timothy Everest in a renaissance. The institution changes commercially and stylistically rather than standing outside fashion.

The publisher confirms reference sections, not their full instructions. NYT reports Sherwood's strict bespoke formulation: hand-measured/cut/sewn, with a hand-cut pattern. Attribute this to the book, not a universal legal standard. No canvassing, fitting-count or measurement tutorial is invented.
The review reports workshop terms: tab for a fussy customer, crushed beetle for a badly made buttonhole. They reveal craft culture and close attention to details. Full glossary not recovered.
The heading exists in the contents list; its actual advice was not recovered.

title: The Italian Gentleman
creator: Hugo Jacomet
note: A map of Italian makers: tailors, cloth merchants, tie makers, shoemakers and other artisans.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
contents.coverage: Profiles of more than fifty Italian houses, with mills and cloth merchants, bespoke tailors, sartorial brands, shirtmakers, ties/umbrellas/gloves and shoemakers. Examples include Vitale Barberis Canonico, Zegna, Rubinacci and Kiton.
contents.caveat: Use the detailed 2017 ISBN 9780500518571 listing. Slovart lists an inconsistent eight-section outline for the same ISBN, including Pitti Uomo; this is not merged into the six-part structure. The author says the book is a selected personal journey, not a complete catalog or academic history.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Strong direct tailoring-school excerpt plus authorized preface; other five maker categories mostly thin.
knowledge.limits: BonneGueule publishes an authorized translated chapter. Regional styles are Jacomet's framework, not guarantees about every modern maker. Legends and interview anecdotes retain their status. No full house profiles or technical buying manual was read.

sections.summary: Three years visiting workshops, factories and shops led to more than fifty selected houses. Jacomet rejects an exhaustive catalog or definitive academic history. It is a personal craft journey, including modest workplaces behind glamorous objects.

The Prandoni-derived ideal is sober and clear-lined, with structured shoulders, a fitted waist and high armholes. Teachers and apprentices transmit it. This distinguishes a geometric outline from softer approaches without supplying universal fitting measurements.

Caraceni's Roman approach uses lighter cloth and less shoulder padding than its British antecedents but retains structure: a geometric shoulder and broad-to-fitted-waist V. It is fluid without simply following natural shoulder contours. The story of Henry Poole garments reaching the family is explicitly a family legend.

The Attolini/Rubinacci account removes weight/internal support. Markers include natural shoulders, little or no lining, shirt-like sleeve insertion with small gathers, a curved boat chest pocket, patch pockets and overlapping cuff buttons. Sleeve fullness aids movement. Softness still requires skilled cutting; these are school markers, not obligatory features of every Neapolitan suit.

Vitale Barberis Canonico and cloth-mill histories appear alongside makers. Finished garments come from a cloth-making system, not just a label. Full mill profiles, fiber grades and fabric specifications were not recovered.

The interview uses Ciro Paone/Kiton to illustrate persistence when workshops were closing. The publisher identifies Rubinacci, Kiton and Zegna with continuity and quality. This is maker history, not an independent ranking or current construction guarantee.
Salvatore Piccolo's shirts/workshop illustrate the section. No full advice on collar proportion, stitches, shrinkage or fitting was exposed.

Marinella's friendliness, early hospitality and roots in Naples, including a declined overseas-shop offer, show service and identity within craft. Tie folds/construction, umbrellas and glove techniques remain unverified.

Enzo Bonafè's recollections of apprenticeship with Amedeo Testoni and shoes for Ronald Reagan show knowledge passed between people/generations. No complete lasts, welt or fit comparison was recovered.

creator: Hugo Jacomet
note: A map of Parisian houses. The reel names Cifonelli, Camps de Luca, Charvet, Berluti and Aubercy.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
contents.status: Bookseller table of contents, compact English edition
chapters: The Parisian Bespoke Tailoring: Cifonelli; Camps de Luca; Francesco Smalto; Berluti Atelier Arnys
Of Men and Shoes: John Lobb; Berluti; Corthay; Aubercy; J.M. Weston; Dimitri Gomez
The Art of Travelling: Louis Vuitton special orders; Moynat Paris
One of a Kind Houses: Maison Bonnet; Marc Guyot; Simonnot Godard; Mellerio
contents.coverage: House-by-house accounts of French tailoring, footwear, shirtmaking, travel goods, perfume and accessories, focused on heritage and craftsmanship.
contents.caveat: English compact edition ISBN 9780500293966; house names and contents may differ in other editions. Promotional claims such as only bespoke eyewear maker are not independently endorsed.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Direct official sample pages support Cifonelli, Smalto, Berluti, Louis Vuitton and Caron profile substance; other sections thinner.
knowledge.limits: Selected sample spreads are not complete profiles. The author confirms compact edition is the same book at smaller size. Glowing profiles are not independent rankings; historic details do not establish current services.

sections.summary: Hand bespoke and a family path from Rome through London training to Paris connect French expression to British technique. The preview says measurements are in inches. P2 mentions four fit/movement principles but does not enumerate them; none are invented here. Training and finishing sustain a house style, rather than nationality alone.

Clear geometric lines and proportion are central. The sample describes a high distinctive lapel notch, a narrower shaped shoulder and specialist workshop skills through fittings. A recognizable signature survives fashion changes. This is a profile, not a universal specification for a suit.

Olga Berluti's patina and artistic choices move beyond conservative convention. Choosing material/color and returning to the atelier involves the owner in a unique object. The profile relates ready-to-wear to bespoke's spirit without equating construction. P3 distinguishes multinational houses from smaller custom makers in the broader section.
Charvet is featured, but no substantive fitting/making passage was exposed. P3 calls shirtmaking coverage limited. No technical collar or stitch rule is invented.

Louis Vuitton special-order craft relates long-lived objects to tradition and modern luxury. The sample contrasts private enjoyment with public status display. Moynat's revived trunk-making is identified by the publisher, but its complete construction account was not read. Neither is a current luggage buying recommendation.

The Daltroff/Wampooille partnership and independent house identity frame Le Tabac Blond's leather interpretation, beyond literal nature imitation. Pour un Homme is another major creation. This is perfume history, not complete application/selection advice or proof of current formulas.
Cartier and S.T. Dupont are in the contents list, but actual chapter advice was not exposed.

The review notes Simonnot Godard's hand-rolled handkerchiefs and Jacomet's personal interest in distinctive makers. Complete technical notes on Maison Bonnet, Marc Guyot, Simonnot Godard and Mellerio were not recovered.

title: Bloomberg Businessweek issue archive
creator: Bloomberg
note: Official browsable grid of issue covers, recent issues back through past years, each linking to its issue page. The direct way to see the current run of covers the reel celebrates.

title: CoverJunkie: Businessweek
creator: CoverJunkie
note: Curated magazine-cover gallery's Businessweek section: recent covers with design commentary and art-direction credits (the January 2026 post credits art director @the.wilkinsonian), plus a 'more from Bloomberg Businessweek' back catalogue.

title: Jordi Ng: Bloomberg Businessweek Covers
creator: Jordi Ng
note: A working Businessweek art director's own selection of covers she art-directed 2022-ongoing (The Egg, Project Maven, The Year Ahead 2024 maze, Cities Issue 2023, A Deepfake Horror Story), each with a note on the commission and illustrator.

title: Internet Archive: Business Week scans
creator: Internet Archive
note: The pub_business-week collection: 1,890 scanned Business Week issues from 1932 onward (SIM microfilm), free to borrow with an Internet Archive account. The full-run vintage counterpart to Bloomberg's official archive, which covers recent years only.

title: EBSCO Bloomberg Businessweek Magazine Archive
creator: EBSCO
note: Billed as the only complete digital backfile: 4,650 issues, 1929-2010, cover-to-cover as originally published. Library/institutional access rather than open web - check a university or public library subscription.

title: magCulture: Bloomberg Businessweek redesigned
creator: Jeremy Leslie (magCulture, 2017)
note: Explains why the 2009-2013 Tyrangiel-Turley Businessweek became an editorial-design touchstone ('a classic blend of restraint and mania', the weekly cover reveal as its own event) and reviews the quieter 2017 redesign under creative director Robert Vargas.

title: designboom: Richard Turley interview
creator: designboom (2013)
note: Turley on the 2010 reinvention in his own words: the redrawn Helvetica, the strict Guardian-learned grid he wanted his 15-person art department to 'fuck up', the Wednesday 7PM ship cycle, and his favorite special issues (2010 year in review, 2011 Steve Jobs, 2012 election).

title: Bloomberg: On the Cover Trail with Richard Turley
creator: Bloomberg LP (2014)
note: Bloomberg's own press piece on the cover team (Turley, assistant CD Tracy Ma, design director Cynthia Hoffman, photo director David Carthas, art director Robert Vargas) and the weekly cover process, citing the mating-airplanes and suicidal-Twitter-bird covers.

title: D&AD: Bloomberg Businessweek Cover Series
creator: D&AD
note: 2016 Wood Pencil winner in Magazine & Newspaper Design. The awards entry states the case for the covers: they 'interpret complex news into succinct visual solutions' and upend what a business magazine cover should be.

title: Richard Turley
creator: Wikipedia
note: Career overview for the creative director behind the famous 2010-2014 era, then MTV, Interview and Civilization. Useful for following where the Businessweek-era designers went next.

title: "Let's Get It On" (United-Continental cover, February 2012)
creator: Bloomberg Businessweek
note: Two planes mounting mid-air for the United-Continental merger story. The most infamous Turley-era cover and one of the covers visible in the reel's frame; Business Insider confirmed in 2012 that the viral image was the real cover.

title: "A Very Long Bull" (September 17, 2018 issue)
creator: Bloomberg Businessweek
note: Bull-market cover whose painted bull is visible in the reel's frame. The official issue page lists the cover story and contents.

title: TasteSkill - anti-slop frontend skills
creator: Leonxlnx
note: Open-source SKILL.md pack billed as "The Anti-Slop Frontend Framework for AI Agents": design-taste skills that steer Claude Code, Cursor and Codex away from boilerplate-looking UI (layout, typography, motion, spacing), plus image-generation skills for reference boards. Installs with npx skills add. The reel's first pick; matches its "apply better design taste using premium references" description.

title: Web Design Guidelines - UI audit checklist (Vercel Labs)
creator: Vercel Labs
note: Vercel Labs' web-interface-guidelines repo: a living, framework-agnostic list of interface decisions (interactions, focus, forms, animation) whose command.md Claude Code skills wrap to audit a UI against modern design principles and catch weak areas before shipping. Matches the reel's "audits your UI" description.

title: AwesomeDesign - directory of DESIGN.md files
creator: AwesomeDesign
note: Directory of real public DESIGN.md files for coding agents (74 in the catalog at check time, from Anthropic's Claude to Vercel, Supabase and Linear): colors, typography, spacing and component specs an agent reads as its design system, matching the reel's "complete design system covering colors, typography, spacing, buttons". Sister site getdesign.md generates a private DESIGN.md from your own site.

title: ImageToCode - design image to frontend code
creator: Leonxlnx
note: The image-to-code skill inside the taste-skill repo: forces an image-first workflow - generate or supply a design reference, analyze its palette, type, spacing and layout, then implement the frontend to match, with rules against cropped boards and card-spam cliches. Matches the reel's "turns design references into usable code". Install: npx skills add leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "image-to-code".

title: Playwright CLI - browser screenshots for coding agents
creator: Playwright (Microsoft)
note: Playwright's official CLI for coding agents: token-efficient browser control (open, type, snapshot, screenshot) so Claude can open the site it built, capture screenshots and catch broken UI, matching the reel's fifth pick. The docs include a Claude Code skill install (playwright-cli install --skills).

title: Persona (1966)
creator: Ingmar Bergman
note: The film behind the reel's shot. Nurse Alma (Bibi Andersson) and actress Elisabet (Liv Ullmann) in a two-hander shot by Sven Nykvist; the two faces are overlapped, by blocking and compositing, into a single face. Criterion lists the cast and Bergman as director; the composite-face reading is the reel creator's description. Criterion also streams it on the Criterion Channel (subscription).

title: The Persistence of Persona (Criterion essay)
creator: Criterion Current
note: Criterion's essay on Persona's lasting hold, opening with the two shots that became its emblems: a boy touching a woman's face on a giant screen, and two women looking at each other in a composite close-up. Best reading to go with the reel. It names Lynch among directors admiring Bergman's work; it does not itself list the specific homages below.

title: La Pointe Courte (1955)
creator: Agnès Varda
note: Varda's first feature, a study of a marriage on the rocks in a fishing village. The reel cites it as an example of the one-sided profile composition used for unrequited love. That pairing is the creator's claim; this entry only verifies the film's pages.

title: Ghost in the Shell (1995)
creator: Mamoru Oshii
note: The reel's example of the shot used for a figuratively and literally shared mind. A fan post compares the recreation frame-by-frame with Persona (user-generated, not an authoritative source); Wikipedia has the film's production background.

title: Mulholland Dr. (2001)
creator: David Lynch
note: One of the two films the reel says directly cites Persona (per the caption; this entry verifies the film page only, not the citation). Criterion has an edition with 4K UHD.

title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019)
creator: Céline Sciamma
note: The other film the reel says cites Persona, with the central-women shot recontextualised (per the caption; this entry verifies the film page only). Criterion also has a Current essay on the film.

title: Vinyl - album art as a turntable on your desktop
creator: shhivv
note: Native macOS app that puts a photorealistic animated turntable on the screen, showing the album art and details of whatever is playing in Spotify or Apple Music (per its site). Matches the reel's first pick. A commenter on the reel says Vinyl isn't free; the maker also sells it through Gumroad. Pricing not checked, and there is an open-source GitHub repo by the same author.

title: Launchy - radial app launcher and switcher
creator: iSapozhnik
note: macOS app giving quick access to launch or switch between applications through a radial menu, which fits the reel's "radial menu" description. Caveat: several unrelated apps are called Launchy (one is a Launchpad replacement at launchy.website); this is the radial one. The reel's "Liquid Glass" claim and exact app match are not confirmed from the video.

title: Droppy - Dynamic Island for the Mac notch
creator: Droppy
note: Mac app that turns the notch (or a floating pill) into a Dynamic Island-style surface: now playing, live activities, shelf and HUDs, with Liquid Glass and animation design written up in its blog. Matches the reel's third pick. The reel says a discount link is in the creator's bio; not checked.

title: Office Romance (2026)
creator: Netflix (Jennifer Lopez, Brett Goldstein)
note: Closest real film to the reel's "office romcom" joke: Netflix's 2026 R-rated rom-com about a secret office romance between two workaholics. Tentative pick: the reel never names a film, it is a skit, and I could not confirm it riffs on this one. A commenter on the reel mentions the SNL comedian Ben Marshall (unconfirmed that he appears in the clip), and another says they searched for where to watch it. Treat as a movie to watch, not an identified source.

title: react-three-fiber - React renderer for three.js
creator: pmndrs (Poimandres)
note: React renderer for the three.js 3D library; the reel's repo 1, shown for building advanced 3D effects on the web. MIT licence, actively maintained. The reel pairs it with Three.js Journey (Bruno Simon's course) as the place to learn the underlying 3D library.

title: liquid-glass-js - Apple-style liquid glass for the web
creator: dashersw
note: WebGL library bringing Apple Liquid Glass-style refraction, blur and masking to web UI elements (buttons, cards, pills); the reel's repo 2, shown with its glass button demo. MIT licence. Owner confirmed from the repo screen recording in the video; a different same-named repo exists, so the exact link matters.

title: shadergradient - customizable animated shader gradients
creator: ruucm
note: Animated, customizable shader-gradient component for React/three.js, also available for Figma and Framer; the reel's repo 3, shown with its customizer UI (shape, motion and colour controls).

title: liquid-logo - liquid-metal effect for any logo
creator: Paper Design
note: Tool that applies a liquid-metal chrome shader to any uploaded logo; the reel's repo 4, shown with chrome logo demos. GitHub lists its licence as "Other", so the caption's own advice to check the licence before reusing code applies here.

title: Tokyo Style
creator: Kyoichi Tsuzuki
note: Photographic record of Tokyo homes as they are lived in: clutter, collecting, improvised storage and personal taste rather than styled interiors. Asia Art Archive describes visits to a hundred homes over two years and eight sections: Beauty in Chaos, The Fancy Fetish, Artsy Pads, The Traditional Touch, Monomaniacs, Kiddie Kingdoms, Inertial Living and Hermitages. The work was first published in 1993; the linked Apartamento edition (2024, reprinted 2025) adds a foreword by Barry Yourgrau and a new afterword by Tsuzuki. The reel does not specify an edition.

title: MAKI OPUS
creator: Fumihiko Maki
note: Career retrospective of architect Fumihiko Maki, published by Thames & Hudson and compiled with his studio. The publisher describes fifty buildings from 1960 onward, including MIT Media Lab, the Aga Khan Museum and 4 World Trade Centre. Coverage follows his materials, building technology and work outside Japan, using archival photographs and drawings. The caption names the publisher, not an author.

title: Dieter Rams: The Complete Works
creator: Klaus Klemp
note: Phaidon's chronological catalogue of the products designed by Dieter Rams, made in collaboration with him and with his foreword. Each product has a description and technical specifications. The publisher situates the work around Rams's ten principles for good design. This is The Complete Works, not the separate title As Little Design as Possible.

title: Eames
creator: Gloria Koenig
note: TASCHEN's Basic Art introduction to Charles and Ray Eames. It covers furniture, architecture, textile design, photography and film, from molded plywood furniture and the Case Study Houses to Powers of Ten. A compact overview of their cross-disciplinary practice, rather than only a chair catalogue.

title: Brett Whiteley: Art & Life
creator: Barry Pearce, with Bryan Robertson and Wendy Whiteley
note: Thames & Hudson survey of Whiteley's work from the 1950s to the final years of his life, with over 180 colour plates. Barry Pearce provides the overview of his life and art; Bryan Robertson writes about the London years; Wendy Whiteley contributes a personal portrait. The publisher emphasizes landscape, the nude and fluid drawing. This is the art survey, not Ashleigh Wilson's biography Art, Life and the Other Thing.

title: Vitra: The Anatomy of a Design Company
creator: Deyan Sudjic, with contributions by Karen Stein and Iwan Baan
note: Phaidon history of three generations behind Vitra and its role across architecture, graphics, photography and product design. Coverage includes work with the Eameses, Gehry and Hadid, support for designers such as Jasper Morrison and the Bouroullecs, preserved design archives and the design museum. The verified edition is published by Phaidon; the caption names Sudjic without naming a publisher.
